before.stem: Which of the following clinical features is NOT typical of a facial nerve palsy:
options: Reduced salivation ie Reduced lacrimal fluid production 8%
before.explanation: Facial nerve palsy can result in inability to close the eye due to paralysis of the orbicularis oculi muscle. Elevation of the eyelid in eye opening is a function of the levator palpebrae superioris muscle and the superior tarsal muscle, innervated by the oculomotor nerve and the sympathetic chain respectively. Vv

after.stem: Which of the following clinical features is NOT typical of a facial nerve palsy:
warnings: Source page and external anatomy reference reviewed; remains an unapproved OCR draft.
after.explanation: Eyelid elevation is supplied by levator palpebrae superioris via CN III and superior tarsal muscle via sympathetic fibres; facial palsy prevents closure, not elevation.
after.learningNote: Eyelid elevation is supplied by levator palpebrae superioris via CN III and superior tarsal muscle via sympathetic fibres; facial palsy prevents closure, not elevation.
after.highYieldNote: Eyelid elevation is supplied by levator palpebrae superioris via CN III and superior tarsal muscle via sympathetic fibres; facial palsy prevents closure, not elevation.

memoryAid.coreFact: Eyelid elevation is supplied by levator palpebrae superioris via CN III and superior tarsal muscle via sympathetic fibres; facial palsy prevents closure, not elevation.

evidence.externalFinding: Facial palsy affects eye closure, while eyelid elevation is not a CN VII function.

options: Uvula deviation away from the affected side
Tongue deviation towards the affected side
before.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve, not the vagus nerve, innervates most of the muscles of the tongue and if damaged may result in tongue deviation on protrusion towards the affected side. . Vv

before.stem: Regarding the glossopharyngeal nerve, which of the following statements is CORRECT:
options: It is the efferent nerve of the gag reflex. 7% (#) t emerges from the cranial cavity through the hypoglossal canal. 4%
It carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. 53%
It innervates the tensor veli palatini muscle. 9% Cv ) It provides parasympatheti secretomotor fibres to the parotid gland. 28%

before.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies parasympathetic secretomotor fibres to the parotid gland, motor fibres to the stylopharyngeus muscle and taste fibres to the posterior one-third of the tongue. before.stem: Regarding the facial nerve, which of the following statements is INCORRECT:
options: Forehead sparing in facial nerve palsy is indicative of a lower motor neuron lesion. (x) The facial nerve supplies taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. 5%
The facial nerve carries parasympathetic fibres to the lacrimal glands.
The facial nerve leaves the brainstem at the cerebellopontine angle.
The facial nerve exits the skull via the stylomastoid foramen.
before.explanation: In facial nerve palsy, if the damage is peripheral (LMN), the forehead will be involved and there will be an inability to close the eyes or raise the eyebrows due to paralysis of the orbicularis oculi and occipitofrontalis muscle respectively. If the damage is central (UMN), there is forehead sparing as the occipitofrontalis and orbicularis oculi muscles have bilateral cortical representation. Vv

after.stem: Regarding the facial nerve, which of the following statements is INCORRECT:
options: Forehead sparing in facial nerve palsy is indicative of a lower motor neuron lesion.
The facial nerve supplies taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
The facial nerve carries parasympathetic fibres to the lacrimal glands.
The facial nerve leaves the brainstem at the cerebellopontine angle.
The facial nerve exits the skull via the stylomastoid foramen.
warnings: Source page and external anatomy reference reviewed; remains an unapproved OCR draft.
after.explanation: Forehead sparing indicates an upper motor neuron lesion; a lower motor neuron lesion involves the forehead.
after.learningNote: Forehead sparing indicates an upper motor neuron lesion; a lower motor neuron lesion involves the forehead.
after.highYieldNote: Forehead sparing indicates an upper motor neuron lesion; a lower motor neuron lesion involves the forehead.
after.mnemonic: UMN spares the forehead; LMN loses the whole side.

memoryAid.coreFact: Forehead sparing indicates an upper motor neuron lesion; a lower motor neuron lesion involves the forehead.
memoryAid.mnemonic: UMN spares the forehead; LMN loses the whole side.

evidence.externalFinding: Bilateral cortical input to the upper facial muscles explains forehead sparing in central lesions.

before.stem: A patient presents with an adducted eye at rest which cannot abduct past the midline, which of the following cranial nerves is most likely to be affected:
options: Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve
warnings: No marked correct option was detected.

before.stem: w A 50 year old man presents to ED with diplopia and a ptosis. On pulling his eyelid up, you note that his pupil is looking down and out, and his pupil is fixed and dilated. Further imaging shows that the patient has a cerebral aneurysm compressing a cranial nerve. Which of the following blood vessels is most likely to be the culprit:
options: Middle cerebral artery & Posterior cerebral artery 9%
before.explanation: Ptosis, fixed dilated pupil and eye resting in down and out position are clinical features of a oculomotor (CN III) palsy. The cisternal portion of the oculomotor nerve is in the subarachnoid space anterior to the midbrain and in close proximity to the posterior communicating artery. Posterior communicating artery aneurysm is an important cause of oculomotor palsy. } Vv
